The Hark investment points to Intel trying to sit closer to AI workloads that could consume its Xeon, packaging and foundry output, rather than only chasing capacity like Nvidia and AMD on the chip side. For an investor, the signal is that Intel Capital is being used as a tool to seed potential future customers for AI servers and x86 based inference instead of a purely financial side bet.

At the same time, this move leans into the very risks analysts already flag, including aggressive capex and foundry losses that rely on strong AI uptake to earn a return. If Hark and similar bets do not translate into disclosed design wins or higher utilization, then Intel's effort to rebuild around AI and foundry growth looks more stretched next to competitors that rely less on owning fabs. Rexielyn Diaz • 5 minute read

Reviewed by: David Hanson

Last updated Nov 2, 2026

AndreyPopov from Getty Images and Kittipong Jirasukhanont from PhonlamaiPhoto's Images via Canva

### Key Takeaways [...] ## Customers are queuing for 2030

CEO Christophe Fouquet was direct in the results release. Supply as currently planned for 2027 and 2028 “will not fully meet the demand of our customers,” he said. Some customers even want to place orders for 2029 and 2030.

So ASML is studying how to push 2028 capacity beyond the 30% increase it had already planned. Meanwhile, low-NA EUV output should reach about 65 systems this year, nearly 50% more than the 44 it shipped in 2025.

Customers are paying ahead to hold their place in line, and that shows up in the cash.

Markets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington.

The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections.

A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022. [...] The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff.

Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale.

Oil fell Monday amid news that both the U.S. and Iran seek diplomatic options to their conflict.

Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for January delivery fell 3.31% to $109.67 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December declined 3.34% to $100.64 per barrel.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force and would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically."

Trump "hasn't made a decision...what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful. But we would prefer to do it peacefully," Rubio said, speaking to reporters over the weekend.

Iranian authorities also signaled that a deal is still possible, following two days of talks mediated by Qatar, as long as demands are implemented tangibly, according to Al Jazeera.

The news come following reports that both the U.S. and Iran are preparing for more military strikes after the midterm elections.

Reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate that the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."

Concerns over the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts will likely linger in the near term.

"Attacks on ships and refineries in the Middle East and on civilians in Ukraine continue, doing little to inspire confidence in the prospects for lasting ceasefires in the foreseeable future," said Tamas Varga, analyst at PVM Oil Associates.

"Nonetheless, hope springs eternal," Varga added.
